lessonTitle: Shape Functions, Mapping and the Jacobian of the Q4 Element

blocks.text: A crankshaft web, a bracket and a pressure-vessel nozzle all have curved or skewed outlines that no rectangle can follow. Isoparametric elements solve this by doing all the mathematics on a perfect square with coordinates between -1 and +1, and then stretching that square onto the real element. The stretch is described by the Jacobian, and its determinant is the first thing to check when a model refuses to run.

blocks.markdown: **Natural coordinates.** The four-node quadrilateral (Q4) is defined on a parent square with natural coordinates $(\xi,\eta)$, each from $-1$ to $+1$ (dimensionless). The nodes are numbered counter-clockwise from the lower-left corner: node 1 at $(-1,-1)$, node 2 at $(1,-1)$, node 3 at $(1,1)$ and node 4 at $(-1,1)$. Each shape function $N_i$ is bilinear, equal to 1 at its own node and 0 at the other three.

blocks.caption: Q4 shape functions in natural coordinates

blocks.title: Isoparametric mapping
blocks.text: An element is **isoparametric** when the same shape functions interpolate the geometry and the unknown field. The physical position of a point is $x=\sum N_i(\xi,\eta)\,x_i$ and $y=\sum N_i\,y_i$ with nodal coordinates $(x_i,y_i)$ in metres, and the displacement is $u=\sum N_i\,u_i$. Because $\sum N_i=1$, the element reproduces any rigid translation and any constant field exactly.

blocks.markdown: **The Jacobian.** To integrate over the real element we need derivatives with respect to $x$ and $y$, but the shape functions depend on $(\xi,\eta)$. The chain rule connects them through the Jacobian matrix $\mathbf J$, whose entries are the derivatives of the physical coordinates with respect to the natural ones (units: metres per unit natural coordinate). We use the convention that the first row differentiates with respect to $\xi$ and the second with respect to $\eta$.

blocks.latex: \mathbf J=\begin{bmatrix}\partial x/\partial\xi&\partial y/\partial\xi\\ \partial x/\partial\eta&\partial y/\partial\eta\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\sum N_{i,\xi}x_i&\sum N_{i,\xi}y_i\\ \sum N_{i,\eta}x_i&\sum N_{i,\eta}y_i\end{bmatrix},\quad \begin{Bmatrix}N_{i,x}\\N_{i,y}\end{Bmatrix}=\mathbf J^{-1}\begin{Bmatrix}N_{i,\xi}\\N_{i,\eta}\end{Bmatrix},\quad dA=\det\mathbf J\,d\xi\,d\eta
blocks.caption: Jacobian matrix, derivative transformation and area scaling

blocks.title: Jacobian of a parallelogram element
blocks.prompt: A Q4 element has nodes (in mm) 1: (0,0), 2: (4,0), 3: (5,3), 4: (1,3). Find the physical position of the centre $(\xi,\eta)=(0,0)$ and the Jacobian matrix and determinant there.

steps.text: At the centre every $N_i=1/4$, so $x=\tfrac14(0+4+5+1)=2.5$ mm and $y=\tfrac14(0+0+3+3)=1.5$ mm.
The determinant is $\det\mathbf J=2(1.5)-0(0.5)=3$ mm$^2$. For a parallelogram it is the same everywhere, and the area is $4\det\mathbf J=12$ mm$^2$, which agrees with base 4 mm times height 3 mm.

rows: Mapping is locally one-to-one and keeps orientation
Element collapsed to a line or a point (for example two nodes coincide)
Fix the geometry; $\mathbf J^{-1}$ does not exist
Element is inverted, folded, or has a re-entrant (reflex) corner or clockwise numbering
Renumber or remesh; stiffness has no physical meaning
blocks.caption: Reading the sign of the Jacobian determinant

blocks.markdown: **Why the sign matters.** The factor $\det\mathbf J$ converts area in the parent square to area in the real element. A negative value means the map has turned the square inside out at that point, so computed areas and strain energies come out with the wrong sign. Because $\det\mathbf J$ of a Q4 varies linearly across the element, its smallest value occurs at a corner, so checking the four corners is sufficient.

blocks.title: A reflex corner gives a negative determinant
blocks.prompt: A Q4 element has nodes (in mm) 1: (0,0), 2: (4,0), 3: (4,4), 4: (3,1), numbered counter-clockwise. Evaluate $\det\mathbf J$ at the four corners and at the centre.

steps.text: Node 4 at (3,1) lies inside the triangle formed by the other three nodes, so the interior angle at node 4 exceeds 180 degrees: the quadrilateral is concave.

Evaluate $\det\mathbf J=x_{,\xi}y_{,\eta}-y_{,\xi}x_{,\eta}$ at each corner using the shape-function derivatives of the Q4. At the corners of nodes 1, 2, 3 and 4 the values are 1, 4, 1, -2 mm$^2$ respectively.
The corner at node 4 has a negative determinant, so the mapping folds over there. At the centre $\det\mathbf J=1$ mm$^2$, which equals one quarter of the area (4 mm$^2$), and is positive.
A positive centre value does not make the element valid. Every Gauss point must have a positive determinant, and the corner check shows this element must be remeshed.

blocks.answer: Corner determinants are 1, 4, 1, -2 mm^2; the negative value at node 4 shows the element is invalid.

items: Write each $N_i$ as the product of two linear factors that vanish on the two edges not touching node $i$, scaled so $N_i=1$ at node $i$.
Differentiate to build $\mathbf J$, then $\det\mathbf J$ and $\mathbf J^{-1}$.
Check the sign of $\det\mathbf J$ at all corners and Gauss points.

blocks.title: Node numbering
blocks.text: Numbering the nodes clockwise instead of counter-clockwise makes $\det\mathbf J$ negative throughout the element, even for a perfect rectangle. Always follow the numbering order your solver requires.

points: Q4 shape functions are bilinear products of $(1\pm\xi)$ and $(1\pm\eta)$ divided by 4; they equal 1 at their node, 0 at the others and sum to 1.
In an isoparametric element geometry and field share the same shape functions, so the Jacobian $\mathbf J$ relates natural and physical derivatives.
$\det\mathbf J$ scales area from the parent square to the real element; at the centre of a Q4 it is a quarter of the element area.
A zero or negative determinant signals a collapsed, folded or wrongly numbered element.

questions.stem: For the four-node quadrilateral in natural coordinates, what is $N_1+N_2+N_3+N_4$ at any point $(\xi,\eta)$ in the element?

options.text: Exactly 1, which lets the element reproduce a uniform field
It depends on $\xi$ and $\eta$, rising towards the centre

questions.correctOptionText: Exactly 1, which lets the element reproduce a uniform field

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the shape functions form a partition of unity, so a field with equal nodal values is reproduced everywhere.
distractorRationale.b: The functions are non-negative on the element, so they cannot cancel.
distractorRationale.c: Each function is 1 at its own node and 0 at the others, and the four always add to 1, so the sum is constant.
distractorRationale.d: The sum is dimensionless; area enters only through $\det\mathbf J$.

questions.explanation: Adding the four products gives $\tfrac14[(1-\xi)+(1+\xi)][(1-\eta)+(1+\eta)]=1$. This is the partition-of-unity property that guarantees rigid-body and constant-field representation.

questions.stem: A Q4 element has nodes at (1,1), (5,2), (6,5) and (0,4) mm, numbered counter-clockwise from the lower-left node. Using the isoparametric mapping, find the $x$-coordinate in mm of the point at $(\xi,\eta)=(0.5,-0.5)$.

The four nodal temperatures of a Q4 element, numbered counter-clockwise, are 100, 140, 180 and 120 degrees Celsius. Using the element's shape functions, what is the interpolated temperature at the element centre $(\xi,\eta)=(0,0)$?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: at the centre every shape function is 1/4, so the value is the average (100+140+180+120)/4 = 135.
distractorRationale.b: This is the value at node 2, not at the centre.
distractorRationale.c: This is the highest nodal value, at node 3; the centre is an average of all four.
distractorRationale.d: This is the value at node 4; at the centre each node has equal weight.

questions.explanation: Each $N_i=\tfrac14(1\pm0)(1\pm0)=\tfrac14$ at the centre, so the interpolated value is the arithmetic mean of the four nodal values. That is $540/4=135$ degrees Celsius.

questions.stem: A rectangular Q4 element is 8 mm long and 5 mm high. Its edges are parallel to the global axes. Find the Jacobian determinant $\det\mathbf J$ (the same everywhere in the element) in mm$^2$.
questions.explanation: For a rectangle $x_{,\xi}=a/2$ with $a=8$ mm and $y_{,\eta}=b/2$ with $b=5$ mm, and the cross terms are zero. So $\det\mathbf J=(4)(2.5)=10$ mm$^2$, which is one quarter of the area 40 mm$^2$.

questions.stem: A Q4 element has nodes (in mm) 1: (0,0), 2: (6,0), 3: (7,4), 4: (1,5), numbered counter-clockwise. Compute $\det\mathbf J$ at the element centre in mm$^2$, using $\mathbf J=[x_{,\xi},\,y_{,\xi};\,x_{,\eta},\,y_{,\eta}]$.
questions.explanation: At the centre $x_{,\xi}=\tfrac14(-0+6+7-1)=3$, $y_{,\xi}=\tfrac14(-0+0+4-5)=-0.25$, $x_{,\eta}=\tfrac14(-0-6+7+1)=0.5$ and $y_{,\eta}=\tfrac14(-0-0+4+5)=2.25$. Then $\det\mathbf J=3(2.25)-(-0.25)(0.5)=6.875$ mm$^2$. As a check, the shoelace area is 27.5 mm$^2$ and a quarter of it is 6.875.

questions.stem: During pre-processing a solver reports a negative Jacobian determinant at one Gauss point of a Q4 element. What does this indicate?

options.text: The element is inverted or has a re-entrant corner there, so the mapping from the parent square folds over
The element is stiffer than expected but otherwise valid
The material has a negative Poisson's ratio
The element is too large and should simply use more Gauss points

questions.correctOptionText: The element is inverted or has a re-entrant corner there, so the mapping from the parent square folds over

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the sign of $\det\mathbf J$ is the local orientation of the map, and a negative sign means the element is turned inside out there.
distractorRationale.b: Negative $\det\mathbf J$ makes the integrated stiffness meaningless rather than larger.
distractorRationale.c: Material properties do not enter the Jacobian, which depends only on geometry.
distractorRationale.d: More Gauss points would sample the same folded map and give wrong results; the geometry must be corrected.

questions.explanation: $\det\mathbf J$ depends only on nodal coordinates and measures the local area scaling with orientation. A negative value indicates clockwise numbering, a folded element or a concave corner, and the mesh must be repaired.

questions.stem: Numbering the nodes of a Q4 element clockwise, instead of counter-clockwise, produces a negative Jacobian determinant even when the element is a perfect rectangle.
questions.explanation: True. Reversing the node order reverses the orientation of the mapping from the parent square, flipping the sign of $\det\mathbf J$ everywhere. The geometry is fine, but the element must be renumbered for the solver.

questions.stem: What is the role of $\det\mathbf J$ when integrating an element stiffness matrix over the real element?

options.text: It converts the area element, $dA=\det\mathbf J\,d\xi\,d\eta$, so the integral can be done on the parent square
It converts displacement in metres into millimetres
It sets the value of Young's modulus used inside the element
It is only needed for triangular elements

questions.correctOptionText: It converts the area element, $dA=\det\mathbf J\,d\xi\,d\eta$, so the integral can be done on the parent square

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the integral over the physical element becomes an integral over the parent square weighted by $\det\mathbf J$.
distractorRationale.b: Unit conversions are unrelated to the Jacobian; it is a coordinate-mapping quantity.
distractorRationale.c: Material properties are independent of the mapping.
distractorRationale.d: The same area scaling applies to any mapped element, quadrilateral or otherwise.

questions.explanation: The stiffness integrand is evaluated in $(\xi,\eta)$, where limits are fixed at $\pm1$, and multiplied by $\det\mathbf J$ to account for the area scaling. The same Jacobian also transforms the derivatives of the shape functions.

questions.stem: Explain why a Q4 element with a negative $\det\mathbf J$ at a Gauss point must be rejected, and describe two mesh situations that cause it.
markingGuide: $\det\mathbf J$ is the local area scaling with orientation, so negative means the mapping is inverted at that point
The integrand of the stiffness is weighted by $\det\mathbf J$, so negative values give negative or wrong-signed strain energy contributions
$\mathbf J^{-1}$ gives wrong derivatives $N_{i,x}, N_{i,y}$, so strains are meaningless
Cause one: clockwise node numbering (or a mirrored element)
Cause two: a re-entrant or badly distorted corner where a node lies inside the triangle of its neighbours, or nodes crossing over
questions.explanation: The determinant controls both the integration weight and the derivative transformation. When it changes sign the stiffness no longer represents a physical element, which is why solvers abort or warn.

questions.stem: Using the requirements that each shape function equals 1 at its own node and 0 at the other nodes of the parent square, and that it is bilinear in $\xi$ and $\eta$, derive $N_3$ for the Q4 element. Then show that $\sum N_i=1$ and state what that implies for the element.
markingGuide: $N_3$ must vanish on the edges $\xi=-1$ and $\eta=-1$ (those not containing node 3)
Sum of all four shape functions $=\tfrac14[(1-\xi)+(1+\xi)][(1-\eta)+(1+\eta)]=1$
Implication: rigid-body translation and a uniform field are represented exactly (partition of unity / completeness)
questions.explanation: Building each function from linear factors that vanish on the opposite edges guarantees the nodal property. The partition of unity then follows from factorising the sum.
